See [Reserved ports](#reserved-ports).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `/run/hopbox`                               | root        | 0755    | every role                      | The sockets: `admin.sock` and `pg/`. `hopboxd run` makes it at each start.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

The install never removes anything under `<data_dir>`.

Root writes and runs what these dirs hold. So the install refuses a dir that another user than root owns, and a dir that is a symlink. It sets the mode of the table on each dir that it makes or finds. A dir that group or others can write thus gets the safe mode back. The host owns three dirs that the install writes into: `/etc/systemd/system`, `/etc/sysctl.d`, and `/usr/local/bin`. The install keeps their mode. If group or others can write such a dir, the install refuses it. `postgres.md` and `sealing.md` give the checks of `<data_dir>/pg` and `<data_dir>/kek`. The data dir itself must be a real dir: mount the file system on it, and do not use a symlink.

### The file system of the data dir

On a server with the node role, `<data_dir>` must be on XFS with reflinks: the node makes the disk of a machine as a reflink copy of its image. The operator makes this file system before the install, with `mkfs.xfs -m reflink=1`, and mounts it on `/var/lib/hopbox` ([Install hopbox on a Debian 13 server by hand](/guide/install-debian/#2-make-the-xfs-file-system)). The Terraform provider makes sure that it is there before its install. If the file system is an XFS without reflinks that holds no file, the provider makes it again ([hopbox Terraform provider](/reference/terraform-provider/#create)).

The install checks the file system before it changes anything. If `<data_dir>` does not exist yet, it checks the nearest dir above it. The install refuses another file system, and XFS without reflinks. The preflight check `reflink` tests reflinks again in `<data_dir>` ([the preflight check](/reference/preflight/)). A server with only the control role has no such rule.

## Releases

Each install and each upgrade keeps two releases: the current one and the previous one. After a good start of `hopboxd`, the install removes every other dir in `/opt/hopbox/releases`. This includes the temp dirs `.incoming-*` of an upgrade that stopped.

A release dir is the release of one bundle. The install checks it before it uses it ([Release bundle](/reference/release-bundle/#checks-of-a-release)). A release dir with the name of a version but another manifest stops the install: two builds of one version never share a name.

The switch of `current` is one rename of a new symlink over the old one. So a reader sees the old release or the new one, never a mix. The same holds for `previous`. The install moves `previous` first and `current` second. So after a crash between the two renames, `previous` still names the release that ran.

The file `/opt/hopbox/.lock` keeps two runs of `install` and `upgrade` apart, with `flock`. A run that finds the lock taken stops at once. `upgrade` holds the lock while it unpacks. It passes the lock to the install of the new release as the file descriptor 3, which the environment variable `HOPBOX_INSTALL_LOCK_FD` names. That install takes the lock on the same open file, so the lock covers the whole upgrade. It then marks the descriptor close-on-exec and removes the variable. So no program that it runs, such as `useradd`, `systemctl`, or Postgres, keeps the lock. The descriptor must be the lock file, and its `flock` must succeed. Otherwise the install refuses it. A descriptor of its own on the lock file is another open file, so it fails while the upgrade holds the lock.

## The image cache

`<data_dir>/images/<hex>` holds one image. `<hex>` is the digest of the image without `sha256:`, for example `images/354fb767...`. A dir holds `artifact.json` and the compressed disk `disk.raw.zst` ([Artifact format](/reference/artifact-format/#digest)).

The install of a node copies the default image of its release into the cache, unless the cache has it already. It writes the copy in a temp dir `images/.incoming-<random>`, checks its digest and the sha256 of its disk, and renames it into place. Then it removes the disk from the release dir. A server without the node role also removes the disk and keeps no image. If such a server gets the node role later, run that install from an unpacked bundle, which has the disk. The install keeps the images of earlier releases, because a rollback needs them. It never removes an image, so the cache grows by about 560 MB with each upgrade that brings a new image. Remove a dir of an image that no release on the server names, and that no machine uses, by hand.

At the first boot of a machine from the image, the node role unpacks the disk to `disk.raw`. Then it checks the disk and removes the compressed copy ([the Firecracker driver](/reference/firecracker-driver/#the-image-cache)). A node can also download the disk of an image that an admin registered with a URL. Its dir then holds only `disk.raw`, and a later install of a release with that image adds its `artifact.json`.

## Users and IDs

| User          | Role                            | What it is for                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `hopbox-pg`   | control, without `postgres.url` | Runs the bundled Postgres, which refuses to run as root ([the bundled Postgres](/reference/postgres/#os-users-and-database-roles)). The name comes from `postgres.user` of the config. |
| `hopbox-jail` | node                            | Holds the user and group IDs of the jailer in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`. No process runs as this user.                                                                           |

The install makes each user with `useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin`, unless the user exists.

The jailer runs the microVM of each machine with its own user ID and group ID. They come from this range:

| Item                                     | Value                          |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| First ID                                 | 1879048192 (`0x70000000`)      |
| Count                                    | 65536                          |
| Last ID                                  | 1879113727                     |
| Entry in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid` | `hopbox-jail:1879048192:65536` |

The range is above the container ranges of systemd (524288 to 1879048191) and below 2^31, a gap that the UID map of systemd leaves unused. `useradd` gives normal users IDs below 60000 and subordinate IDs below 600100000. The entry in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid` tells every other tool of the host that the range is taken. The install adds the entry with `usermod --add-subuids` to the file that lacks it, and with `--add-subgids` to the other, so no file gets it twice. If another entry of `/etc/subuid` or `/etc/subgid` overlaps the range, the install refuses it. The same holds for a user of `/etc/passwd` or a group of `/etc/group` with an ID in the range.

## systemd units

### hopboxd.service

```ini
[Unit]
Description=hopbox server
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
RequiresMountsFor=/var/lib/hopbox


[Service]
Type=notify
ExecStart=/opt/hopbox/current/hopboxd run --config /etc/hopbox/hopboxd.toml
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
TimeoutStartSec=180s
TimeoutStopSec=105s
KillMode=mixed
LimitNOFILE=1048576
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=full
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
LockPersonality=yes


[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

| Setting                                                               | Why                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Type=notify`                                                         | When every unit of the process is ready, `hopboxd run` sends `READY=1` ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#run)). So `systemctl start` and `systemctl restart` return only at that time. If `hopboxd` exits first, they fail. An install and an upgrade depend on this. |
| `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=5s`                                 | If a unit fails, `hopboxd` exits with status 1, and systemd starts it again after 5 s.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `TimeoutStartSec=180s`                                                | The first start migrates the control store. Postgres alone has 60 s to start.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `TimeoutStopSec=105s`                                                 | With every role, the stop timeouts of the units of `hopboxd` add up to 104.1 s. With the control role and the node role, they add up to 98.1 s ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#run)).                                                                               |
| `RequiresMountsFor=/var/lib/hopbox`                                   | `hopboxd` starts only after the file system of the data dir is mounted. Without it, a slow mount at boot lets `hopboxd` write into the empty dir below the mount point.                                                                                            |
| `NoNewPrivileges=yes`                                                 | No process of the unit can gain privileges through a setuid program. `hopboxd` runs as root and only drops privileges, for example for Postgres.                                                                                                                   |
| `KillMode=mixed`                                                      | systemd sends `SIGTERM` to `hopboxd` alone, and `hopboxd` stops Postgres in order. A `SIGTERM` to every process of the unit stops Postgres out of order.                                                                                                           |
| `ProtectSystem=full`                                                  | `/usr`, `/boot`, `/efi`, and `/etc` are read-only for the unit. `hopboxd run` writes only the data dir and `/run/hopbox`. `hopboxd install` and `hopboxd upgrade` run outside the unit, so they still write `/etc/hopbox` and `/opt/hopbox`.                       |
| `ProtectHome=yes`                                                     | `/home`, `/root`, and `/run/user` are empty for the unit.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `PrivateTmp=yes`                                                      | The unit has its own `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `ProtectKernelModules=yes`, `ProtectKernelLogs=yes`                   | No process of the unit loads a kernel module or reads the kernel log. The kernel still loads the modules of nftables by itself.                                                                                                                                    |
| `ProtectControlGroups=yes`                                            | The cgroup tree is read-only for the unit. The unit of each machine gets its cgroup from systemd, over D-Bus.                                                                                                                                                      |
| `ProtectClock=yes`, `ProtectHostname=yes`                             | No process of the unit changes the clock or the host name of the server.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `RestrictSUIDSGID=yes`, `RestrictRealtime=yes`, `LockPersonality=yes` | No process of the unit makes a setuid or setgid file, takes a realtime priority, or changes its execution domain.                                                                                                                                                  |

The acceptance suite passes on the [tested server](/reference/preflight/#the-tested-server) with these settings, through the boot, the restart policy, and the delete of real machines. Two settings stay off, because the node role needs what they block:

* `ProtectKernelTunables`: the node network writes sysctls at its start, such as `net.ipv4.ip_forward` ([the node network](/reference/node-network/)).
* `PrivateDevices`: the driver makes the tap device of each machine through `/dev/net/tun`, and the node checks `/dev/kvm`.

The jailer and Firecracker run in the unit of each machine, not in this unit.

### hopbox-machines.slice

```ini
[Unit]
Description=hopbox machines


[Slice]
```

The microVM of each machine runs in its own transient unit in this slice, `hopbox-machine-<id>.service`, not in `hopboxd.service`. [The Firecracker driver](/reference/firecracker-driver/#the-unit-of-a-machine) lists the properties of such a unit. A restart or an upgrade of `hopboxd` stops only the processes of `hopboxd.service`, so the microVMs keep running. The slice has no `[Install]` section: systemd starts it with the first unit in it. At a shutdown of the server, systemd stops `hopboxd.service` first, then each unit in the slice, and each guest shuts down cleanly ([the Firecracker driver](/reference/firecracker-driver/#a-stop-through-systemd)).

The install writes each file whose content changed. Then it runs `systemctl daemon-reload`. It runs `systemctl enable hopboxd.service` on each run.

## Reserved ports

The SSH ports of the machines are 10000 to 30000. The kernel must not give them to an outgoing connection of the host. So the install of a server with the node role reserves them in two places:

| Place                                        | What the install does                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/etc/sysctl.d/60-hopbox.conf`               | Writes `net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports = 10000-30000`, which `systemd-sysctl` applies at each boot. The setting covers IPv4 and IPv6.                  |
| `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_reserved_ports` | Adds `10000-30000` to the list of the running kernel, and keeps the ports that the list holds already. If the list covers the range, it changes nothing. |

The drop-in sets the whole list. If another drop-in sets this key with a name that sorts after `60-hopbox.conf`, that drop-in wins at boot.

The disk listener of a node reserves no port either. It listens on port 7444 of the mesh address only ([Cold move](/reference/cold-move/#the-disk-listener)).

The DNS role reserves no port. It listens on the ports of `dns.listen`, port 53 by default ([the bootstrap config of hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd-config/#keys)). The edge role reserves no port either. It listens on `edge.https_listen`, `edge.http_listen`, and `edge.ssh_listen`, ports 443, 80, and 2222 by default. At its start, it also replaces the nftables table `inet hopbox_edge`, which sends the SSH ports 10000 to 30000 to `edge.ssh_listen`. A stop deletes the table ([the SSH front door](/reference/ssh-front-door/#redirect-of-the-ssh-ports)). The redirect matches only new connections, so an edge server without the node role needs no reserved ports.

## The bootstrap admin API key

Before any control role runs, the Terraform provider makes a random admin API key. It passes only the hash of the key to the install of the first server. `hopboxd install --bootstrap-admin-key-hash` writes the hash to `<data_dir>/bootstrap-admin-key.sha256`. Only the install that makes the Postgres cluster of the server writes the file. A later run ignores the flag and logs a warning. So a later run can never bring back a key that an admin revoked.

| Item           | Value                                                                              |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Content        | The SHA-256 of the whole admin API key, as 64 lowercase hex digits, then a newline |
| Owner and mode | root, 0600                                                                         |
| Role           | control only                                                                       |

The file is the hand-off from the install to the control role. The install writes the file and needs no running control role and no admin call for the key. The `store` unit of `hopboxd run` reads the file after the migrations ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#run)):

| Case                                                                                                                                                                           | What the control role does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The install has no admin API key.                                                                                                                                              | It registers the hash as the admin API key `bootstrap`, with a lifetime of 90 days. It calls `RegisterAdminKey` as the caller `local_root` of the `hopboxd` process. The audit log gets `admin_key.register`. Then it removes the file and logs `registered the bootstrap admin API key`. |
| The install has an admin API key already, expired or not.                                                                                                                      | It removes the file unused and logs a warning, so a stale file never adds a key.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| The file is wrong: not a regular file, not of the user of `hopboxd` (root on a server), or not mode 0600. Or it does not hold 64 lowercase hex digits and an optional newline. | It registers nothing, keeps the file, and logs an error. The start goes on.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

The key text itself never reaches the server. [CLI tokens, API keys, admin API keys, and SSH keys](/reference/credentials/#admin-api-keys) shows how to make a key and its hash.

# Sessions, cookies, and sign-in links

> The session cookie, the lifetimes, the check against cross-site requests, the magic links and login links, what a sign-in does, and the rate limits.

A person signs in to the console of an install with a magic link, with GitHub, or with Google. On the first day, the first instance admin signs in with a first-admin login link. A sign-in starts a session, and a cookie holds the session in the browser. This page gives the cookie, the lifetimes, the check against cross-site requests, the recent sign-in, the form of the links, the link of a new sign-in method, and the rate limits. [The sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/) lists the calls. [Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/) covers the sign-in with GitHub and Google. [CLI tokens, API keys, admin API keys, and SSH keys](/reference/credentials/) covers the credentials of the hopbox CLI, scripts, and SSH clients. The code is in `internal/auth`, `internal/service`, and `internal/api`.

## Lifetimes

| Credential                                                            | Lifetime                                                                     | Use                                                                                               | Source                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Session                                                               | 30 days after the sign-in. After 7 days without a call, it ends before that. | many calls                                                                                        | A phase 1 default                                         |
| Recent sign-in of a session                                           | 10 minutes after the sign-in                                                 | the calls that need it, such as the Admin area of the console ([Recent sign-in](#recent-sign-in)) | A phase 2 default                                         |
| Magic link                                                            | 15 minutes                                                                   | once                                                                                              | the same                                                  |
| First-admin login link                                                | 15 minutes                                                                   | once                                                                                              | the same                                                  |
| Flow of a sign-in with GitHub or Google                               | 10 minutes                                                                   | once                                                                                              | [Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#start) |
| Invitation to an org                                                  | 7 days                                                                       | once                                                                                              | [The org API](/reference/org-api/#invitations)            |
| Code of a private machine URL                                         | 60 seconds                                                                   | once                                                                                              | [The edge role](/reference/edge/#private-machine-urls)    |
| Token of a private machine URL, in the cookie `__Host-hopbox_machine` | as long as the session that made it                                          | many requests                                                                                     | [The edge role](/reference/edge/#private-machine-urls)    |

All times use the clock of Postgres. A session records its last use at most once per minute, so the idle time of 7 days is exact to one minute. In maintenance mode, a session records no use ([the API server](/reference/api/#maintenance-mode)). Only a call that passes the check against cross-site requests records a use ([Calls with the cookie](#calls-with-the-cookie)).

## Tokens

Each session, magic link, login link, and invitation to an org carries a token. So does the state of a sign-in with GitHub or Google. A token is 32 random bytes, in base64url without padding, so 43 characters. The control store keeps only the SHA-256 of a token ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#sessions)). A copy of the database thus signs nobody in. The audit log never holds a token, and the server never logs one.

A token of another form never matches a stored hash, so the server refuses it before any lookup.

## The session cookie

A sign-in sets this cookie:

```text
Set-Cookie: __Host-hopbox_session=<token>; Path=/; Expires=<end>; Max-Age=<seconds>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
```

| Attribute               | Value                                             | Reason                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Name                    | `__Host-hopbox_session`                           | With the `__Host-` prefix, the browser keeps the cookie only from a secure origin, with `Path=/` and without `Domain`. So the cookie belongs to the host of the install only, and never reaches a machine URL such as `box1.example.com`. The edge also drops each cookie whose name starts with `__Host-hopbox_` from the requests to a machine and from its answers ([the edge role](/reference/edge/#private-machine-urls)). |
| `Path`                  | `/`                                               | The prefix needs it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `Expires` and `Max-Age` | the end of the session, 30 days after the sign-in | At the end of the session, the browser drops the cookie. The server also ends an idle session.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `HttpOnly`              | set                                               | Scripts of the page cannot read the token.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `Secure`                | set                                               | The browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `SameSite`              | `Lax`                                             | The browser sends the cookie with a link from another site, but not with a form post or a script call from another site.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

`SignOut` and `DeleteAccount` clear the cookie with `Max-Age=0`. They also end the private machine URLs of the session: the delete of the session deletes their tokens, and the edge servers check each URL again ([the edge role](/reference/edge/#private-machine-urls)). A browser sends a cookie on its own, also after its session ended. So a cookie that names no live session counts as no cookie, and the response clears it. A stale cookie thus never blocks the next sign-in.

## Calls with the cookie

The session resolver of the request gate reads the cookie ([the API server](/reference/api/#request-gate)). A call that carries the cookie must also pass this check against cross-site request forgery:

1. The `Origin` header is the origin of the install: `https://` and the domain of the install, for example `https://example.com`. The API and the console share this origin.
2. The call uses the Connect protocol, with the header `Connect-Protocol-Version: 1`.

A form or a link of another site can send neither. A script of another site can send the Connect header only after a CORS preflight, and hopbox grants none. A machine URL such as `https://box1.example.com` is another origin, so a page that a machine serves cannot act with the cookie either.

The gate resolves a call with the cookie in these steps:

| Case                                                                                                   | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| The call has no session cookie.                                                                        | The session resolver passes the call to the next resolver.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| The token names no live session: unknown, malformed, signed out, idle for 7 days, or past its 30 days. | The cookie counts as absent, and the call goes on as for a request without it. The response clears the cookie, unless the call sets a new one, as a sign-in does. A call that needs a credential then gets `unauthenticated` with the message `this call needs a credential`.                    |
| The session is live, but the call fails the check above.                                               | `unauthenticated` with the message `the credential is not valid`. The response keeps the cookie, so a page of another site cannot sign anybody out. The log record `api credential refused` has the reason, for example `the Origin header "https://evil.example" is not "https://example.com"`. |
| The install has no domain.                                                                             | `unauthenticated`, as above. Without a domain, the install has no origin to trust.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| The control store does not answer.                                                                     | `unavailable` with the message `the server failed to check the credential. Retry later`.                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| The session is live, and the call passes the check.                                                    | The caller is `session`, with the account, the session, whether the account is an instance admin, and whether the sign-in is recent. The gate reads the instance admin role on each call, so a revoke takes effect at once. The call records the use of the session.                             |

So a cookie call through gRPC, gRPC-Web, or a Connect GET request fails. The console uses Connect POST requests.

A WebSocket is the one exception to step 2. A browser cannot add a header to a WebSocket. So a request with the header `Upgrade: websocket` passes with the `Origin` header of step 1 alone (`auth.CheckWebSocketRequest`). This is safe, because only the WebSocket API of a browser sends that header, and it always sends the true origin of the page. Only the endpoint `/api/ws/exec` takes a WebSocket ([the machine API](/reference/machine-api/#the-websocket-endpoint)).

The calls that set the cookie, `VerifyMagicLink` and `VerifyLoginLink`, must pass the same check, also without a cookie. Otherwise a page of another site can sign a browser in to an account of its choice. A call that fails it gets `permission_denied` with the message `the request does not come from the console of the install: ...`, and the link stays unused.

The callback of a sign-in with GitHub or Google also sets the cookie. The provider sends the browser to it from its own site, so it cannot pass the check. The state cookie of the browser takes the place of the check ([Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#callback)).

## Recent sign-in

A session counts as recent for 10 minutes after its sign-in. The time of the sign-in is the column `created_at` of the session ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#sessions)). The use of a session does not change it, so only a new sign-in makes a session recent again. The gate reads it with the clock of Postgres on each call.

A call that a session taken over must not reach needs a recent sign-in. These calls need one:

| Call                                                                                                                                                                                          | Reason                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ApproveDevice` ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#approvedevice))                                                                                                   | The approval makes a CLI sign-in whose refresh token lives 30 days and renews with each use. So the CLI sign-in can outlive the session.                                                         |
| `RequestMagicLink` with `link` ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#requestmagiclink))                                                                                 | The link adds a sign-in method to the account. The method outlives the session.                                                                                                                  |
| `GET /auth/{provider}/start?link=1` ([Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#link-to-a-signed-in-account))                                                                         | The same. This endpoint is not a call of the API. It sends an older session to the sign-in page of the console instead of an error.                                                              |
| Each call of the admin API that a session can make ([the admin API](/reference/admin-api/#admin-sessions)), the reads too                                                                     | An instance admin operates the whole install. A session lives for days in a browser, so the Admin area of the console works only for 10 minutes after each sign-in.                              |
| `ListAuditEntries` with `whole_install`, or for an org in which the instance admin is not an owner or an admin ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#listauditentries)) | An instance admin reads these audit logs as in the Admin area. A CLI token of an instance admin reads them without this rule. An org owner or org admin reads the log of its own org without it. |

The rule applies only to a console session, because only a session has a sign-in in a browser. Such a call gives these results:

| Caller                                                           | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A session whose sign-in is at most 10 minutes old                | The call goes on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| A session whose sign-in is more than 10 minutes old              | `permission_denied` with the message `permission denied: this action needs a sign-in within the last 10 minutes. Sign in again, then retry`, and the detail `hopbox.v1.RecentSignInRequired` with `max_age` 10 minutes ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#recentsigninrequired)).              |
| Any other caller, such as a CLI token, an API key, or local root | The check of the sign-in passes it, and the policy of the call decides. For example, `ApproveDevice` takes only a session. So a CLI token or a key gets the policy refusal `permission denied: a caller of kind <kind> may not do auth.approve_device`, without the detail. An anonymous caller gets `unauthenticated`. |

Only the refusal of an old session has the detail. So a client knows from the detail that a new sign-in fixes the error. The other calls of an old session keep working. On the admin API, the session of an account that is not an instance admin gets the refusal of the policy without the detail. A new sign-in does not change that refusal.

To get a recent sign-in, the person signs in again in the same browser. The new sign-in ends the old session of that browser and starts a new one ([What a sign-in does](#what-a-sign-in-does)). The sessions of the account in other browsers stay. The console shows the sign-in page for this with `/signin?again=1` ([Console](/reference/console/#sign-in)).

The policy check enforces the rule for the admin API and for `ListAuditEntries` ([the API server](/reference/api/#callers-and-policy)). Their rules allow the session of an instance admin only with a recent sign-in. A rule can refuse a session with an older sign-in, and allow the same session with a recent one. In that case, `policy.Authorize` returns the error of this section. `ApproveDevice`, `RequestMagicLink` with `link`, and the start of a link with GitHub or Google call `service.RequireRecentSignIn` after their policy check. Both checks refuse only a session with an older sign-in, so an admin key and local root keep the calls that their policy allows.

## Magic links

A magic link is a sign-in link that hopbox sends by email. It needs the domain of the install, and the SMTP config of the install ([SMTP config](/reference/smtp/)). A dev or test install can use the file mail transport in place of the SMTP config ([Mail](/reference/mail/#the-file-transport)).

```text
https://example.com/auth/email#token=<token>
```

The token is in the fragment, after `#`. A browser never sends the fragment to a server. So the token stays out of the access logs of servers and proxies, and out of `Referer` headers. The console page `/auth/email` reads the token and calls `VerifyMagicLink`.

The email has this form:

```text
From: hopbox <no-reply@example.org>
To: ann@example.org
Subject: Sign in to example.com


Open this link to sign in to example.com:


https://example.com/auth/email#token=<token>


The link works once, for 15 minutes. If you did not ask for it, you can ignore this email.
```

The server sends the email in the call, after the link commits, and waits at most 20 s for the SMTP server. With the file transport, the server writes the email to a file in `<data_dir>/mail` and sends nothing.

A link that adds an email to an account has another subject and text ([Link a new sign-in method](#link-a-new-sign-in-method)):

```text
From: hopbox <no-reply@example.org>
To: ann.work@example.org
Subject: Add your email to your account on example.com


Open this link to add ann.work@example.org as a sign-in method of your account on example.com:


https://example.com/auth/email#token=<token>


Open it in the browser where you asked for it. The link works once, for 15 minutes. If you did not ask for it, you can ignore this email.
```

### Rate limits

`RequestMagicLink` counts the links of the last hour in the control store, so the limits hold across every control server.

| Limit                 | Value       | Error                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Links for one email   | 5 per hour  | `resource_exhausted`: `too many requests: this email got the most sign-in links of an hour. Use one of them, or wait` |
| Links from one client | 20 per hour | `resource_exhausted`: `too many requests: this client asked for the most sign-in links of an hour. Wait, then retry`  |

A client is one IPv4 address, or one IPv6 /64, because one IPv6 host often holds a whole /64. An IPv4 address in IPv6 form counts as its IPv4 address. The address is the peer of the request. Behind the edge, the peer is the address of the client that the edge forwards. Only a server with the edge role can name it ([the internal listener](/reference/internal-listener/#forwarded-requests)). The limit of a client skips a loopback peer, such as `127.0.0.1` or `::1`. A loopback peer is a process or an SSH tunnel on the same server, on the API listener. It stands for every client, so a limit on it blocks everyone. Each request takes a transaction lock (`LockKeyMagicLinks`, [the bundled Postgres](/reference/postgres/#advisory-lock-keys)), so requests at the same time cannot pass a limit together. A request whose email fails to send still counts. A link of an email to an account counts as a magic link ([Link a new sign-in method](#link-a-new-sign-in-method)). The messages never say how many links an email got, so they tell nothing about the activity of others.

## First-admin login links

`sudo hopboxd admin login-link --email <email>` prints a login link ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#admin-login-link)). The link is for the first instance admin of a new install, which has no SMTP config and no OAuth app yet.

```text
https://example.com/auth/login-link#token=<token>
```

The console page `/auth/login-link` reads the token and calls `VerifyLoginLink`. The link works once, for 15 minutes. It needs the domain of the install.

## What a sign-in does

Each sign-in proves an identity: a method and an email. It then reaches one account:

1. If the account of an earlier sign-in holds the method, the sign-in reaches that account. A magic link names its method by the email. A login link names its method by the email too, apart from magic links. GitHub and Google name their method by the subject at the provider, so a new email at the provider reaches the same account.

2. Else, the method can prove the email, and an account can hold that email as verified. If that account has no identity of a provider, the sign-in links the method to it. An identity of a provider is a method of GitHub or Google. A magic link proves its email. GitHub and Google prove the email that the provider verified, and nothing else passes ([Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#providers)). A login link proves no email.

   If the account has an identity of a provider, the sign-in fails and changes nothing. Then only a link from a session adds a method to the account ([Link a new sign-in method](#link-a-new-sign-in-method)). The error is `failed_precondition` from `VerifyMagicLink`, or `409` at the callback of [Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#errors), with this message:

   ```text
   the sign-in conflicts with a sign-in method of the account: the account of dana@example.org signs in with GitHub or Google, so a new sign-in method joins it only through a link. Sign in with a method of the account, then link Google on the account page. If you lost every method of the account, the operator removes the lost one with hopboxd admin account sign-in-method remove
   ```

   The rule protects an account against a lapsed domain. The new owner of the domain can prove an old address of the account, with a magic link or at a provider. The email of a method follows the provider, so a rule by email misses an old address. So once the account has an identity at a provider, the email alone links nothing. A person who lost every method of the account gets help from the operator ([Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#recover-a-lost-identity)).

3. Else, the sign-in creates an account with the email, the method, and a personal org named `Personal`, with the account as its owner. A magic link, GitHub, and Google mark the email verified. A login link leaves it unverified. GitHub and Google also give the account the name of the person at the provider as its display name. The display name stays empty for a name that breaks the rules of [Domain rules](/reference/domain-rules/#display-names). At GitHub, an empty name falls back to the login.

So the email of a login link never links to another account. A magic link, GitHub, or Google with the same email reaches another account. A second login link for the same email reaches the account of the first one. A verified email belongs to at most one account.

A sign-in also does these steps:

* A login link makes the account an instance admin. An account that is one already stays one.
* A sign-in from a browser that has a session ends that session. The new one replaces it.
* It starts a session and records the sign-in in the audit log ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#audit-entries)). A link of a method to an account by its verified email gets its own entry.

A refused link writes the log record `sign-in link refused` at level info, with `component=service` and `kind`, never the token. A refusal for a reason other than the token has the field `reason` too: `another session asked for the link`, or `the account needs a link for a new sign-in method`.

Two first sign-ins with one email at the same time make one account: each sign-in takes a transaction lock (`LockKeySignIn`).

## Link a new sign-in method

A person who is signed in adds a new sign-in method to the account. Once the account has an identity of GitHub or Google, this is the only way in for a new method. The console offers it on `/account` ([Console](/reference/console/#pages)). Each link needs a session with a recent sign-in ([Recent sign-in](#recent-sign-in)).

| Method           | Start                                                                                                                                               | End                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Email link       | `RequestMagicLink` with `link` and the email ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#requestmagiclink)). The email gets a link. | The person opens the link in the same browser. `VerifyMagicLink` with the session of the request adds the email method. |
| GitHub or Google | The browser opens `/auth/<provider>/start?link=1` ([Sign-in with GitHub and Google](/reference/oauth/#link-to-a-signed-in-account)).                | The callback of the provider comes back with the same session, and adds the identity.                                   |

A link needs a recent sign-in when it starts. From then on, it binds to its session for its lifetime, so it ends also after those 10 minutes. A link binds to the session that started it. The link works only with the session cookie of that session, so the same browser must open it. Another browser, another session, or a browser without a session gets `permission_denied` from `VerifyMagicLink`, and the link stays unused. At the callback of a provider, another caller gets `400`. A sign-out ends the session, so its links never work after it. A link that ends after its session ended fails with `unauthenticated`: `this call needs a credential: the session that started the link ended. Sign in again, then link the method again`, or `403` at the callback. A magic link then stays unused. So a person cannot add a method to the account of another person, also with the mailbox of that person.

A link starts no session and sets no cookie. The session of the browser stays. A link does these steps in one transaction:

1. It takes the transaction lock `LockKeySignIn`, and checks that the session is still live. A share lock on the session row keeps a sign-out from ending it before the link commits.
2. It refuses a method that signs in to another account: `failed_precondition`, or `409` at the callback. The message names the method, for example `this Google identity signs in to another account. Remove it from that account first`.
3. It refuses a method that the account has: `already_exists`, or `409` at the callback. `RequestMagicLink` refuses an email method of the account before it sends the mail.
4. It refuses an email that another account holds as verified: `failed_precondition` with `the email kim@example.org is a verified email of another account, so it signs in only to that account`. The method of an email decides where a magic link of that email signs in. So without this step, the holder of the mailbox could move the magic links of another account to the own account.
5. It refuses a second identity of the same provider: `the account already signs in with another GitHub identity. Remove that method first, then link the new one`.
6. It adds the method. The email of the method becomes a verified email of the account. For an identity of a provider, this step skips an email that another account holds as verified. An unverified email of the account, such as the email of a login link, becomes verified.
7. It writes the audit entry `account.link_sign_in_method` ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#audit-entries)). If the account is an instance admin, the entry is a notice to the instance admins, and hopbox sends its email after the commit ([the admin API](/reference/admin-api/#notices-to-instance-admins)).

A link of GitHub or Google needs no match between its email and the emails of the account. The session proves the account, and the provider proves the identity. So a login-link account, whose email is unverified, can link GitHub or Google (plan question Q23).

## Sweep

Every 10 minutes, the leader deletes the ended sessions. It also deletes the magic links, the login links, and the flows of GitHub and Google that are older than 24 hours ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#leader-jobs)). It deletes the codes of machine URLs that expired before their trade too. The delete of a session also deletes the tokens of the machine URLs that it made ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#machine_url_sessions)). A link stays after its use for the rate limits. The same sweep deletes the ended CLI sign-ins and the old device sign-ins ([CLI tokens, API keys, admin API keys, and SSH keys](/reference/credentials/#sweep)).

# SMTP config

> The SMTP config that sends the sign-in links: its fields, TLS modes, the sealed password, and its errors.

hopbox sends magic links and invitations to orgs by email through the SMTP server of the install ([the org API](/reference/org-api/#invitations)). An instance admin sets the server through the admin API: `sudo hopboxd admin config smtp set` on a control server ([hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd/#admin-config-smtp-set)), or the call `SetSMTPConfig` ([the admin API](/reference/admin-api/#setsmtpconfig)). Without an SMTP config, the install sends no sign-in links, and `GetInstallInfo` does not list `SIGN_IN_METHOD_EMAIL_LINK`. An invitation then gives its link only to the inviter. The code is in `internal/mail`, which uses [go-mail](https://github.com/wneessen/go-mail).

The install uses the SMTP config while its mail transport is `smtp`, the default. A production install uses SMTP. A dev or test install without an SMTP server can write each mail to a file instead, with the transport `file` ([Mail](/reference/mail/)). That transport keeps the SMTP config, and does not use it.

## Fields

The fields of the SMTP config live in the row of `install_config` ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#install_config)). A change of the SMTP config adds 1 to the version of the install config.

| Field    | Type                         | Default                        | Rule                                                                                                                                           |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| host     | string                       | none, required                 | A host name of at most 253 characters, or an IP address. It has no port, no spaces, and none of `/ : @ [ ]`, except in an IPv6 address.        |
| port     | integer                      | the usual port of the TLS mode | 1 to 65535.                                                                                                                                    |
| TLS mode | `starttls`, `tls`, or `none` | `starttls`                     | See [TLS modes](#tls-modes).                                                                                                                   |
| username | string                       | empty                          | The SMTP login. A username needs a password, and a password needs a username.                                                                  |
| password | string                       | empty                          | The SMTP password. It needs the TLS mode `starttls` or `tls`, so that it never travels in plain text. hopbox seals it ([Password](#password)). |
| from     | string                       | none, required                 | The sender of the mail, such as `no-reply@example.org` or `hopbox <no-reply@example.org>`, in the form of RFC 5322.                            |

With a username, hopbox logs in with the strongest mechanism that the server offers, for example `SCRAM-SHA-256` before `PLAIN`.

## TLS modes

| Mode       | Usual port | What it does                                                                                                              |
| ---------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `starttls` | 587        | Connects in plain text, then requires `STARTTLS` before it sends anything else. A server without `STARTTLS` gets no mail. |
| `tls`      | 465        | Speaks TLS from the first byte (implicit TLS).                                                                            |
| `none`     | 25         | Never encrypts. Use it only for a relay on the same host or network. It allows no password.                               |

With TLS, hopbox needs TLS 1.2 or later, and checks the certificate of the server against the system roots and the host name.

## Password

hopbox seals the password with envelope encryption ([Sealing](/reference/sealing/)). The place of the value is the install secret `smtp.password`. So a sealed password that someone copies into another column does not open. Only the column `install_config.smtp_password` holds it.

A seal needs a key-encryption key. On a new install without one, `SetSMTPConfig` with a password fails with `failed_precondition` and the hint `Run hopboxd admin kek rotate to make the first one`.

The admin API never returns the password. `GetSMTPConfig` returns only `password_set`. `SetSMTPConfig` without a password keeps the password that is set now, for example to change the sender. A kept password never goes to another server or login: a change of the host or the username needs the password again. The audit log records `password_changed`, never the password.

hopbox opens the password for each email that it sends, and keeps it in memory only for that send. A rotation of the key-encryption key leaves the password sealed by the old key, until a rewrap moves it ([Sealing](/reference/sealing/#rewrap)).

## The DNS records of the sender

The DNS role of hopbox serves only the records of hopbox in the zone of the install. So send mail from an address in another zone that you control, such as `no-reply@example.org` for the install `example.com`. Set SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for that zone at its DNS provider. Without them, many mail servers put the sign-in links in the spam folder.

## Mail that hopbox sends

| Mail            | When                                                                                                                                  | Content                                                                                                         |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Magic link      | `RequestMagicLink` ([the sign-in, account, and audit API](/reference/auth-api/#requestmagiclink))                                     | [Sessions, cookies, and sign-in links](/reference/sessions/#magic-links)                                        |
| Invitation      | `CreateInvitation` ([the org API](/reference/org-api/#createinvitation))                                                              | The org, the role, the link, and the end of the link                                                            |
| Security notice | A call that leaves something that lasts, such as `CreateAdminKey` ([the admin API](/reference/admin-api/#notices-to-instance-admins)) | What changed, who did it, when, the ID of the audit entry, and how to undo the change. It never holds a secret. |

Each mail is plain text in UTF-8, with a `Date` and a `Message-ID` ([Mail](/reference/mail/#the-mail-that-hopbox-sends)). hopbox connects with a timeout of 15 s for the connection and each reply. A send waits at most 20 s in all.

## Example

```sh
printf '%s\n' "$SMTP_PASSWORD" | sudo hopboxd admin config smtp set \
  --host smtp.example.org --username hopbox@example.org --password-stdin \
  --from 'hopbox <no-reply@example.org>'
```

```text
host  smtp.example.org
port  587
tls  starttls
username  hopbox@example.org
password_set  true
from  hopbox <no-reply@example.org>
mail_transport  smtp
version  3
update_time  2026-10-16T09:09:37Z
```

## Errors

| Error                                                                                                                                      | Cause                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: the host is empty`                                                                                 | No host.                                                                         |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: the host "<host>" is not a host name or an IP address`                                             | The host has a port, a space, or another character that a host name cannot have. |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: the port <n> is not 1 to 65535`                                                                    | A bad port.                                                                      |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: give both a username and a password, or neither`                                                   | A username without a password, or the reverse.                                   |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: a password needs the TLS mode starttls or tls, so that it never travels in plain text`             | A password with the TLS mode `none`.                                             |
| `invalid argument: invalid SMTP config: the sender address "<from>" is not an email address: ...`                                          | A bad sender.                                                                    |
| `invalid argument: a new host or username needs the password again`                                                                        | A new host or username without a password, while a password is set.              |
| `failed precondition: the keyring has no key-encryption key to seal or open the value. Run hopboxd admin kek rotate to make the first one` | A password on an install without a key-encryption key.                           |

# The SSH front door

> The SSH front door of the edge role: its listener, the redirect of the SSH ports, the keys, and the sign-in. Also the connection to a machine, the channels, the checks, the limits, AuthorizeSSH, metrics, and logs.

The SSH front door is the SSH endpoint of the edge role. A client reaches a machine at the SSH port of that machine on an edge server, with an SSH key of its account. The user name is the Linux user in the machine. The front door checks the key with the control role. Then it opens its own SSH connection to the OpenSSH server in the machine, and it forwards the channels of both sides. It never runs a shell on the edge server itself.

This page covers the listener, the redirect of the SSH ports, the keys, and the sign-in. It also covers the connection to the machine, the channels and the requests that pass, and the checks of an open connection. Then it covers the limits, `EdgeService.AuthorizeSSH`, the audit entries, the metrics, and the logs.

The front door is in `internal/edge/sshfd`. The keys, the check of a key, and the host keys of the guests are in `internal/service/sshfrontdoor.go`. The control role pushes the keys in `internal/control/channel/edge.go`.

In the examples, the domain of the install is `example.com`, and the machine `box1` has the SSH port 10022.

## Listener

| Item                            | Value                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Address                         | `edge.ssh_listen` of the bootstrap config. Default: `:2222`, port 2222 on every address ([the bootstrap config of hopboxd](/reference/hopboxd-config/#keys)). The port must be outside 10000 to 30000. With the redirect, the listener takes every address, because the redirect sends each connection to the address of the interface that took it. |
| Redirect                        | `edge.ssh_redirect`, true by default. `hopboxd` then sends every TCP connection to a port from 10000 to 30000 of the server to the listener ([Redirect of the SSH ports](#redirect-of-the-ssh-ports)).                                                                                                                                               |
| Protocol                        | SSH 2. The version string is `SSH-2.0-hopbox`. The key exchanges, the ciphers, and the MACs are the defaults of `golang.org/x/crypto/ssh`.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Open connections                | At most 16,384. A connection past the bound waits in the backlog of the kernel.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Open connections of one client  | At most 64. A client is an IPv4 address, or the /64 of an IPv6 address. The front door closes a connection past this bound at once.                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Handshake timeout               | 30 s from the TCP connection to the end of the sign-in.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Sign-in tries of one connection | At most 6, as `MaxAuthTries` of OpenSSH.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

The unit `edge` of `hopboxd run` opens the listener with the HTTPS and HTTP listeners ([the edge role](/reference/edge/#listeners)). If another program holds the port, the start fails, and `hopboxd` exits with status 1. The error names the address, such as `sshfd: listen on :2222: bind: address already in use`.

At a stop, the unit ends every SSH connection first. An SSH connection cannot move to another process, so the client sees the connection close. Then the unit removes the redirect.

## Redirect of the SSH ports

Each machine has its own SSH port on the edge servers, from 10000 to 30000 ([Domain rules](/reference/domain-rules/#ssh-ports)). The port names the machine before the SSH handshake. With `edge.ssh_redirect`, `hopboxd` replaces the nftables table `inet hopbox_edge` at the start of the edge role with this table:

```plaintext
table inet hopbox_edge {
  chain prerouting {
    type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat;
    fib daddr type local tcp dport 10000-30000 redirect to :2222
  }
  chain output {
    type nat hook output priority dstnat;
    fib daddr type local tcp dport 10000-30000 redirect to :2222
  }
}
```

The chain `prerouting` takes the connections of other hosts. The chain `output` takes the connections of the server to its own addresses, such as `ssh -p 10022 127.0.0.1` on the server. In both chains, the match `fib daddr type local` takes only a connection to an address of the server itself. So the traffic that the server forwards keeps its port, such as the egress of machines and of containers. The outgoing connections of the server to other hosts keep their ports too. One netlink batch replaces the table, so no connection sees a part of it. A stop of the edge role deletes the table first, before it ends the connections.

The front door reads the port that the client dialed from the connection tracking of the kernel (`SO_ORIGINAL_DST`, or `IP6T_SO_ORIGINAL_DST` for IPv6). A connection that no rule moved, such as one to port 2222 itself, has the port of the listener. The front door closes a connection whose port is outside 10000 to 30000 at once. When conntrack records the redirect, the host firewall takes the connection on the port of the listener ([the host firewall](/reference/host-firewall/#ports)). So a connection from outside the server to port 2222 itself gets no answer.

The redirect needs Linux, the kernel module `nf_tables`, and `CAP_NET_ADMIN`. `hopboxd.service` runs `hopboxd` as root ([Server layout](/reference/server-layout/#hopboxdservice)). On a system without nftables, such as macOS, the edge role logs a warning and serves only its own port. A connection to that port is outside the SSH ports, so it reaches no machine there. With `edge.ssh_redirect = false`, the operator makes the redirect. A connection then reaches the front door with the port that the client dialed, as the kernel tracks it.

A flush of the nftables ruleset also drops the table `inet hopbox_edge`, and with it every SSH port. So every 2 s, the front door checks its table: the table, its chains `prerouting` and `output`, and one rule in each. If a part is gone, it installs the table again, and logs `the nftables table inet hopbox_edge lost a part outside hopboxd, so the SSH front door installed it again. Do not flush the nftables ruleset of an edge server` at level error. A stop of the edge role ends the checks before it removes the table.

`hopboxd install` keeps the SSH ports out of the ports of outgoing connections on a server with the node role ([Server layout](/reference/server-layout/#reserved-ports)). The redirect matches only new connections, so the answers to an outgoing connection of the edge server never reach the front door.

## Keys

The install has two Ed25519 keys for the front door. Both are the same on every edge server and never change.

| Key        | Use                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Host key   | The front door shows it to every client on every SSH port. `GetInstallInfo` returns its public key in `ssh_host_key` ([the API server](/reference/api/#installservice)). The hopbox CLI writes it to `~/.ssh/known_hosts` under the name `hopbox-<domain>`, and the managed SSH block sets `HostKeyAlias hopbox-<domain>` ([hopbox CLI](/reference/cli/#ssh-files)). So the first connection never asks the user about the host key. |
| Client key | The front door signs in to the OpenSSH server of each machine with it. Each machine spec carries its public key in `authorized_keys`. The guest agent writes it to `/etc/hopbox/authorized_keys`, and sshd reads that file for every Linux user ([hopbox-guest](/reference/hopbox-guest/#files)).                                                                                                                                    |

The first control process that starts with a key-encryption key makes both keys. It seals the private keys with the places `InstallSecret{Name: "ssh_host.key"}` and `InstallSecret{Name: "ssh_client.key"}`, and stores them in the table `ssh_front_door_keys` ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#ssh_front_door_keys)). The rewrap of `hopboxd admin kek rewrap` moves both ([Sealing](/reference/sealing/)). Without a key-encryption key, the control role logs `the install has no keys of the SSH front door yet` at its start, and `ssh_host_key` stays empty.

The control role pushes both private keys to each server with the edge role after the first heartbeat of each control channel, in `EdgeSSHKeys` ([the control channel](/reference/control-channel/#edge-pushes)). Before the first key-encryption key, each heartbeat tries again, so the keys reach the edge soon after the first `hopboxd admin kek rotate`. The edge role keeps them only in memory. Before they arrive, the front door closes each connection before the handshake.

## Sign-in

The client signs in with a public key. Every other method fails.

1. The client offers a public key without a signature. The front door says yes to every key, and asks the control role nothing. So the public part of a key tells nobody whether it opens a machine.
2. The client signs with the key. The front door checks the signature.
3. The front door refuses a certificate, and a user name that is not a Linux user name ([User name](#user-name)).
4. The front door takes one try from each bucket: the bucket of the client, of its network, and of every client ([Limits](#limits)).
5. The front door refuses a key that holds 64 open connections already ([Limits](#limits)). So such a key never reaches the control role, and writes no audit entry.
6. The front door calls `EdgeService.AuthorizeSSH` with the SSH port, the public key, the user name, and the IP address of the client.
7. The front door checks that the routes of the edge name the same machine at the port. It takes one slot of the key. Another sign-in of the same key can take the last slot between steps 5 and 7, so the front door checks the bound here again.

Every refusal is the same for the client: `Permission denied (publickey)`. If the client has another key, it then tries that key.

The refusals take different paths in the control role. An unknown key needs one read of the control store. A known key also needs the read of the machine of the port. So the time of an answer can tell the holder of a valid key which ports hold a machine. It tells nothing about the machines of other accounts beyond that, and a key of nobody learns nothing.

### User name

The user name of the connection is the Linux user in the machine. It has 1 to 32 characters: lowercase letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Its first character is a letter or `_`. Examples: `user`, `root`, `_apt`. The main user of the default image is `user` ([Default image](/reference/default-image/)). The OpenSSH server of the machine decides whether the user exists and can sign in.

The control role refuses a user name that looks like a credential, such as `hbx_dev` or `ghp_` and 20 letters. The audit entry of a sign-in names the user, and the audit log refuses such a value ([Control store tables](/reference/control-store/#record-an-entry)).
